title: The US midterm elections and this Norman Rockwell painting
summary: Following the historic victory of Democratic Senator-elect Scott Colom in the US midterms, it would have been nice to visit the Freedom Summer marker to remember three voting rights activists—to say,…

blocks.text: The US midterm elections, especially in Mississippi where Democratic challenger Scott Colom became the state’s first Black senator since 1874, reminded me of this painting by Norman Rockwell.

It depicts the final moments of three young men: voting rights activists James Chaney, a 20-year-old Black Mississippi native, and two Jewish New Yorkers, Michael Schwerner, 24, and Andrew Goodman, 20. They were kidnapped, beaten and killed by Klu Klax Klan members in June 1964 for taking part in the campaign to register Black voters in Mississippi.

blocks.caption: DEFIANCE. Norman Rockwell’s painting “Murder in Mississippi,” depicts a defiant civil rights advocate Michael Schwerner (in white shirt), with his colleague, a wounded Black Mississippi local James Chaney clutching his arms, facing a US deputy sheriff and Klan conspirators holding guns (only thei…

blocks.text: Michael Schwerner, in white shirt, is shown holding his colleague in the voting rights campaign, a wounded Mississippi local James Chaney. Another colleague in the campaign, Anthony Goodman, is lying face down on the ground.
There’s a look of defiance on Schwerner’s face. What was he thinking shortly before he too was gunned down?
They were killed the day after I was born in Manila. That’s one reason what happened to them resonated with me — even though I didn’t know about them until I moved to California in my ’20s.

blocks.caption: The US midterm elections and this Norman Rockwell painting

blocks.text: I first heard their names in Mississippi Burning, which drew heavy criticism for downplaying the stories of Chaney, Goodman and Schwerner and the activists of the Freedom Summer campaign. FBI agents, played by Gene Hackman and Willem Dafoe, were the heroes in the movie. (READ: Actor Gene Hackman and wife found dead alongside dog at home)

I learned more as a student at the UC Berkeley Graduate School of Journalism where we watched Jon Else’s documentary Eyes on the Prize. The series led me to read Taylor Branch’s books bout the Civil Rights movement, Parting the Waters, Pillar of Fire, and At Canaan’s Edge.

blocks.caption: The US midterm elections and this Norman Rockwell painting

blocks.text: Years later, I came across Race Beat: The Press, The Civil Rights Struggle and the Awakening of A Nation, by the legendary journalist Gene Roberts and Emory University professor Hank Klibanoff. The winners of the Pulitzer Prize in 2007, this powerful book is an account of the US Civil Rights movement through the eyes of the journalists who covered it.
I spent a bit of time in the South last summer.

My family and I spent a week in Alabama to celebrate my son’s graduation from Army flight school at Fort Rucker. We visited our other son in New Orleans where he lived while interning at the NASA Space Center in nearby Mississippi. We celebrated the Fourth of July in the New Orleans Riverfront and watched fireworks on the Mississippi River. (READ: Letting go on the road to Idaho: Notes on fatherhood)
I had one regret about my summer in the South, which became more pronounced after the midterms.

Just a two-hour drive from New Orleans, at the intersection of County Road 515 and State Highway 19 near Philadelphia, Mississippi, there’s a plaque marking the area where James Chaney, Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner were killed.

blocks.caption: KILLED. Newspaper clipping shows voting rights advocates Michael Schwerner, James Chaney, and Andres Goodman. Courtesy of Normal Rockwell Museum YT

blocks.text: I had thought of driving there to see it. But that didn’t happen.
It would have been nice to visit the marker, to remember James Chaney, Michael Schwerner and Andrew Goodman. To say, “Thank you.” – Rappler.com
(This article was first published in the author’s LinkedIn.)

Benjamin Pimentel is a journalist and technology editor based in the San Francisco Bay Area. His novel, ‘Mga Gerilya Sa Powell Street,’ won the 2007 National Book Award for Fiction and was staged by the Cultural Center of the Philippines’ (CCP) Tanghalang Pilipino in 2008.
